To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) the simulation of queueing network can prematurely block owing buffer exhaustion, (ii) buffer exhaustion can occur in simulators of queueing networks, whether or not they are stable, and (iii) buffer exhaustion can be prevented by compactification and interprocessor flow control.

(i) the distributed simulation of a network of FCFS servers can prematurely block, (ii) this blocking can be prevented by compactification, and (iii) this blocking can also be prevented by using interprocessor flow control.

(1) for the conservative and optimistic synchronization protocols the distributed simulation of the queueing network can get blocked owing to event buffer exhaustions; (2) compactification, when used in combination with interprocessor flow controls, prevents event buffer exhaustions in the distributed simulation of a queueing network; and (3) the resulting algorithm is nonblocking.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the distributed simulation of a class of queueing networks that are known to have a number of interesting and useful properties.
the distributed simulation of a queueing network with irreducible MarkOVian routing, which is a general model that can represent many real systems.
the development of nonblocking distributed algorithms for the simulation of FCFS FCFS queueing network models.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
we have presented an algorithm that is deadlock-free, nonblocking, and nonpreemptable for the simulation of FCFS networks of infinite buffers, and Markovian routing.
the simulation of a network of FCFS queues with Markovian routing, when using the algorithms proposed in this paper, cannot block due to buffer exhaustion.
the algorithm proposed is a nonblocking algorithm for distributed simulation of FCF S queueing networks with infinite buffers, irreducible Markov routing and finite memory.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

, for the class of networks under consideration, the distributed simulation algorithms proposed here have the desirable property of being deadlock free, and that they can be used to simulate networks with arbitrarily many processors.

we have developed a general algorithm, based on compactification, for the distributed simulation, with the conservative and optimistic synchronization protocols, of queueing networks that are stable and have finite buffers.
we have presented the first distributed algorithm for simulating FCFS queueing systems that can be guaranteed to be deadlock-free.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the distributed simulation of general queueing networks can lead to premature deadlock, which is not possible with the distributed simulation of feedforward networks.

, in general, one cannot prevent deadlock owing to buffer exhaustion by using interprocessor flow control and compactification alone, and that, in general (i.e., for arbitrary networks), one needs a nonblocking algorithm for simulating queueing networks.
the problem of buffer exhaustion in simulating FCFS queueing network is not restricted to the case when the simulator is unstable.
